proof.criterion: Acceptance 1, second half: the front door arrangement is asserted rather than described — one tailnet node, one listener, each reachable only from the workloads that may dial it, and both other workloads ordered behind the front door — proved at the input shape the consuming stack actually passes.
proof.surface: The same Construct server, constructed with the consuming stack's own inputs (existingNamespace: true, allowedNamespaces: [envoy, legion], namespace: dispatch) rather than the component suite's defaults, at replicas 3 and at the default.
proof.command: EXISTING_NAMESPACE=true ALLOWED_NAMESPACES=envoy,legion NAMESPACE=dispatch REPLICAS=3 ./head/dump, then jq over the Deployments' dependency lists, the Services, the NetworkPolicies and the pod templates
proof.observed: 34 registrations and no Namespace object. NetworkPolicy example-dispatch carries two ingress rules on 8766 — the namespaceSelectors envoy and legion, and podSelector app=example-dispatch-tailnet — so Serve still reaches the app when a namespace is named; example-dispatch-tailnet admits 1055 from app=example-dispatch and app=example-dispatch-listener alone; example-dispatch-listener admits 9020 from app=example-dispatch alone; no rule carries an empty from, a namespaceSelector on the two new policies, or an ipBlock. Both the app and the listener Deployments list the front door's Deployment and its Service URNs in RPC dependencies, and the front door itself waits only on the cluster, so there is no cycle. The front door keeps serviceAccountName=example-dispatch, TS_KUBE_SECRET=example-dispatch-tailscale-state and TS_HOSTNAME=example-dispatch, and binds TS_SOCKS5_SERVER=0.0.0.0:1055; each workload's pods wear app=<its own name> alone, so Service example-dispatch selects the app's pods only. The app's ENVOY_TOKEN and the listener's ENVOY_API_TOKEN both resolve to secretKeyRef example-dispatch-listener/ENVOY_API_TOKEN. A non-default namespace (dispatch-two) moves the Serve proxy target, ENVOY_NATS_SOCKS5_PROXY and ENVOY_URL with it, so none of the three cluster-local addresses is pinned to the default namespace.
proof.negativeControl: An envoyImage bump changes Deployment example-dispatch and Deployment example-dispatch-listener and leaves Deployment example-dispatch-tailnet byte-identical, and a tailscaleImage bump changes only example-dispatch-tailnet: the ordinary release does not roll the tailnet node every reader arrives at, and a front-door change does not roll the app.

The app Deployment's metadata.name, metadata.namespace and spec.selector.matchLabels are byte-identical to the base's — the fields whose change would make the consumer's preview a replacement — and its logical Pulumi name is unchanged, so the resource keeps its URN. unproven: No surface in a Legion pod reaches a cluster or the consuming stack's Pulumi state, so nothing of the deployed behaviour is proved at this head. What that leaves unproven, for the next issue's preview and apply to settle: (1) Tailscale Serve under TS_USERSPACE=true resolving and dialling the app's cluster DNS name, the one claim in the design with no in-repo proof; (2) the cutover apply briefly running two tailscaled processes against the one state Secret, with the consumer's auth key already spent (the implement handoff's APPLY NOTE: back the Secret up first, and mint the key Reusable going forward — the consuming program currently mints it Reusable: false); (3) whether a rolling update actually loses no request — envoy-dispatch's server.Shutdown closes its listener as soon as SIGTERM arrives and no pod carries a preStop delay, so a connection arriving in the endpoint-propagation window can still be reset, which only a measured release will show; (4) the front door's 100m CPU / 128Mi reservation, now carrying every app replica's NATS traffic as well as all tailnet traffic, which nothing here measures.

An ordinary release — a new envoyImage — recreates the listener Deployment as well as rolling the app, because the listener runs the same image and is Recreate at one replica by design. For that window envoy-dispatch's calls to the listener (comment delivery to an agent session, session and role lookups) fail; they are recorded as failed delivery attempts with a cause and a Retry rather than lost, and the window is strictly shorter than the base's, where the whole app pod was down. The infra README covers it in one clause ("so is every update of the front door or of the listener, at any replica count"); a reader looking only at "its readers see no gap" could miss that an app image bump is also a listener update.
observations: Coverage gap, not a defect: TestDispatchNetworkPolicyAdmitsOnlyTheGivenNamespaces reads ingress[0] alone, so a change that replaced the front-door rule instead of appending it when allowedNamespaces is set — the production configuration — would keep the suite green while leaving Serve unable to reach the app at any port. The tester exercised that exact shape and both rules are present today; extending that test to assert the second rule would close it.

replicas is refused below 1 and has no ceiling: 2147483648 renders as spec.replicas and would be refused by the API server at apply (the field is int32), and a fractional 3.7 sent over the wire by a non-Go consumer is truncated to 3 by the property unmarshaller. Neither is reachable from the generated Go SDK, whose Replicas is *int, and neither is a realistic operator value.

Pre-existing, untouched by this change: the listener's environment is rendered inside an ApplyT that panics rather than returning an error when core.ListenerConfig.Env refuses (for example a natsUrl that bus.LocalNATSURL vouches for, which conflicts with the SOCKS5 proxy). The base panics on the same inputs, since its SOCKS5Proxy was likewise non-empty.
scrubEvidence: Not applicable: this issue's acceptance criteria call for no environment or secret-scrub evidence. The rendering was checked for secret handling all the same — the listener bearer reaches both pods as a secretKeyRef and never as a literal, and the generated passwords appear in the dump only under their secret wrapper.
